ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Miami, FL
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging and UT weld inspection for Miami port, marine, cold storage and utility steel. Atlantis NDT mobilizes to site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing and UT Inspection in Miami, Florida
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic testing (UT) in Miami, Florida, with an emphasis on what salt air does to steel: remaining-wall thickness surveys on hulls, tanks, piping, crane structures and pilings, and angle-beam examination of welds in plate, pipe and structural members. Technicians are mobilized to your yard, plant, terminal or building site for the agreed scope. Describe the asset, material and governing code, then request a UT quote for Miami. We reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Miami

Miami is a port, a marine-service center and a gateway for perishable cargo, and each of those puts steel in contact with chloride. PortMiami moves cruise passengers and containers, which means ship-to-shore crane structures, mooring hardware, fender systems and the steel of terminal buildings. The Miami River supports a working cluster of vessel repair and marine service yards, where hull plate, tanks and deck structure are measured before repairs or sales. Superyacht refit work adds another demand for gauging on steel and aluminum craft.

Away from the water, the airport district maintains fuel storage, hydrant lines and ground support equipment. Cold storage and food distribution facilities handle imported produce, flowers and seafood, so ammonia refrigeration piping and vessels are everywhere in the western suburbs. Hotels, hospitals and data centers run chilled-water loops that are rarely shut down. The utility and the county water and sewer department operate tanks, clarifiers and pipe racks that stay wet most of the year. Wall loss is the shared concern, and UT answers it directly.

What UT finds and what it cannot see

An ultrasonic probe sends a pulse of sound into the metal and times its return. For a thickness survey the interval between the entry pulse and the back-wall echo converts to remaining wall. For weld examination, an angled beam travels through the weld metal and reflects from internal planar flaws: lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, cracks and slag lines. UT reaches below the surface and works on carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminum and most other metals that carry sound.

It is not a surface method and it is not always practical. Thick marine coatings, heavy marine growth and rust scale scatter the beam, and the surface must usually be cleaned back to sound metal at each test point. Pitting is a particular trap in Miami: a probe covering a wide area can read the sound metal beside a pit, so the technician uses a small probe and watches the A-scan. Coarse castings and stainless welds attenuate sound and may call for a different method or a modified technique. Where UT is not the right answer, the quote says so.

Corrosion in a salt and humidity climate

Miami's air carries chlorides year-round and its humidity rarely drops, so carbon steel corrodes under coatings, at coating breaks, at crevices and underneath insulation. Corrosion under insulation is a common reason for piping and vessel surveys here: moisture enters through damaged jacketing, sits against the steel and corrodes it out of sight. UT thickness readings at selected locations, taken after insulation is cut back at suspect spots, show whether wall has been lost before a leak does. Hull plate, tank bottoms and the splash zone of pilings face the same attack from the outside.

Chloride also affects stainless steel, which can pit or crack where it is welded, stressed or sheltered from rain. UT is not the first method for surface-breaking cracking, so a survey on stainless often pairs thickness readings with penetrant testing in Miami. For carbon steel attachments and lugs, magnetic particle testing in Miami is the natural companion. The plan should set the mix of methods before crews are mobilized so each visit covers everything that needs to be checked.

Thickness surveys: grids, locations and probes

A repeatable survey begins with a location plan. On a tank shell the technician lays out a grid of courses and positions; on piping the plan uses condition monitoring locations (CMLs) at elbows, tees, reducers and low points; on a vessel the heads, nozzles and shell courses each get points. Every location is numbered, cleaned and read, and the readings are logged against the same numbers in the next survey so a corrosion rate can be calculated from real change and not from noise.

For corroded surfaces the preferred tool is a dual-element probe with a calibrated step block of the same material. High-temperature probes and couplant handle hot lines. On thin or pitted wall, the A-scan display shows whether a reading is the true back wall or a double echo. The reference standards are ASTM E797 and, for work under ASME Section V, SE-797 in Article 23. Our ultrasonic thickness requirements guide explains the Section V requirements.

Weld examination with shear-wave probes

Where a weld needs volumetric examination, the technician scans with angle-beam probes, usually 45, 60 or 70 degrees chosen for thickness and joint geometry. A distance-amplitude curve built from side-drilled holes in a matching calibration block sets the reference level, and scanning covers the weld and heat-affected zone from the sides the joint allows. Each indication is located by depth and position along the weld, sized by length and amplitude, and compared with the code's acceptance table.

In Miami, weld UT shows up on crane booms and runway girders at the port, on thick-plate structural connections in building frames, on pressure piping in process and utility plants, and on repairs to steel craft. ASME Section V Article 4 gives the technique for pressure work, AWS D1.1 covers structural steel with its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and AWS D1.5 governs steel bridges built for the state transportation department. The ultrasonic testing guide covers the physics in more depth.

Codes, Florida rules and the authorized inspector

The code that governs the item sets the technique and the limits: API 653 for aboveground storage tanks, API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping, ASME Section VIII Division 1 (Appendix 12 for UT of welds) and ASME B31.3 (paragraph 344.6 and Table 341.3.2) for new construction. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record, and our part is the examination: calibrated readings and a clear record the inspector can rely on.

Florida adds its own layer. The Division of State Fire Marshal's Bureau of Fire Prevention runs the Boiler Safety Program, which administers the Boiler Safety Act in chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes and Rule 69A-51 of the Florida Administrative Code. A thickness survey on a boiler in a Miami hotel, hospital or plant may support that inspection. Process facilities with covered chemicals, ammonia refrigeration among them, are also subject to OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119, and its mechanical integrity requirement for inspection and testing.

Hulls, pilings and the splash zone

Marine steel corrodes fastest where wet and dry meet. On a hull that is the waterline and the boot-top area; on a dock or seawall it is the splash zone of a steel piling or sheet pile; on a crane runway near the quay it is the lower flange that stays damp. Thickness readings in these zones are taken at a closer spacing than on the dry upper structure, because wall loss is uneven and a coarse grid can miss the worst spot. Where fouling or coating cannot be removed in the water, readings are taken at haul-out or from the dry side of a plate.

Who performs and approves the work

We keep no office in Miami. Technicians are mobilized to the site for the agreed scope and work under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician calibrates, examines and interprets; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. For Miami work the approving Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Because the employer is the certifying body under SNT-TC-1A, the written practice and each technician's record are part of the documentation you can request with the report.

Employers who run their own programs can use Level III consulting for procedure writing and audits.

What the UT report contains

The report identifies the asset, its location in the facility or yard, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe, calibration block and calibration checks, and the technician and level. Thickness data comes as a grid or CML sketch with each reading, the nominal wall, the minimum required wall and the lowest reading found, plus any areas that could not be read. Weld data lists every indication by position, depth, length and amplitude against the reference level, with an accept or reject decision against the named table. Surface condition, coating state and any limitations are written down, so a later survey can compare like with like.

Planning a UT job in Miami

Several Miami-specific factors shape the schedule. Hurricane season runs from June through November, and crews should expect weather holds and, after a storm, a queue of urgent inspections of cranes, tanks and structures. Heat and sun are daily problems: dark steel surfaces get far hotter than the air, so tank shells and deck plate are often read early or shaded, and couplant for hot surfaces should be on the list. Afternoon thunderstorms close outdoor jobs quickly, and humidity causes flash rust on freshly cleaned steel, so cleaning and gauging should be done close together.

Port and airport work needs facility-arranged credentials and escorts, and vessels in a yard need hot-work, confined-space and gas-free arrangements before anyone enters a tank. Scaffolding, lifts and insulation removal are the owner's responsibility unless the quote says otherwise. Because technicians travel to Miami, grouping locations into a single visit, and stating up front who supplies access and power, avoids repeated mobilization.

UT, MT or PT for your Miami job

If the question is how much wall remains, or whether a weld has an internal flaw, use UT. If the worry is a surface crack in steel, such as a toe crack on a lifting lug, choose MT. If the part is stainless or aluminum, or you must prove a ground-out area is crack-free, choose PT. Many marine and process repairs combine UT for the volume with MT or PT for the surface. The national UT page shows the full scope, and the MT versus PT comparison helps with the surface-method choice.

Training your own UT technicians

Miami employers who want in-house capability can enroll technicians in UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 training and let them practice on the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator. The NDT training page for Miami explains the course structure, and the NDT practice tests give candidates a way to check their knowledge before an employer examination.

faq.q: Can UT measure steel thickness on a ship or yacht in Miami?
faq.a: Yes, on steel and many aluminum hulls, provided the surface is clean at each reading point. Marine growth, thick coatings and rust must be removed locally. The technician maps readings to frames or plate locations so repairs can be planned from the data.

faq.q: Why does Miami corrosion need dual-element probes?
faq.a: Salt-driven corrosion leaves rough, pitted surfaces where single-element probes struggle. Dual-element probes handle roughness and near-surface echoes better, and the technician checks the A-scan so a pit or a double echo is not mistaken for sound wall.

faq.q: Is corrosion under insulation a problem for Miami piping?
faq.a: It is a frequent cause of wall loss here. Warm, humid, salt-laden air gets under damaged jacketing and keeps the steel wet. UT readings at selected locations, taken after insulation is opened at suspect spots, show the actual remaining wall.

faq.q: Does UT meet Florida boiler inspection needs?
faq.a: UT can supply thickness data that supports a boiler inspection, but state requirements under chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes and Rule 69A-51 remain with the owner and the state or commissioned inspector. We deliver readings the inspector can use.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be used on welds at the port?
faq.a: Yes. Crane booms, girders and thick structural connections are routine candidates for angle-beam examination under AWS D1.1 or the contract code. The procedure is written for the joint geometry, with a reference curve built from side-drilled holes.

faq.q: What should I arrange before UT technicians come to Miami?
faq.a: Arrange safe access, lifts or scaffolding, insulation removal at test points, cleaned contact surfaces, drawings or location maps, and any facility credentials. For tanks and vessels, include confined-space and gas-free permits. A pre-job call settles responsibilities.

faq.q: How do hurricanes affect inspection scheduling in Miami?
faq.a: Weather holds are likely from June through November. After a storm, owners often need fast checks of cranes, tanks and steel structures, so it helps to agree scope, access and a call-out plan before the season starts instead of during an emergency.

faq.q: Does Atlantis operate an office in Miami?
faq.a: No. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. The quote states what the travel and access requirements are, and the Level III approval, procedures and reports follow the same process as for work anywhere else.

faq.q: Can my staff learn UT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training with simulator practice and practice tests. The employer certifies its own staff under its written practice, so the course is one part of the qualification record.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Miami, FL | MT & MPI
mt.description: On-site magnetic particle inspection of port cranes, lifting gear, vessel welds and structural steel in Miami, Florida. Wet and dry MT. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Miami, Florida
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle testing (MT, or mag particle inspection) in Miami, Florida, on carbon and low-alloy steel that works hard in a salt-air environment: crane structures and lifting gear at the port, boat hoist and travel lift frames, vessel attachment welds, hull and deck repairs, and structural steel connections. Technicians are mobilized to your site with yokes and particle materials. Send us the part, the material and the code, then request an MT quote for Miami. We reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Miami

Lifting equipment is the clearest case. PortMiami runs ship-to-shore and yard cranes, and every hook, shackle, pin, padeye and boom connection on them is loaded repeatedly in a corrosive atmosphere, which is exactly the situation where fatigue cracks start at weld toes. The boatyards and marine service operations on the Miami River depend on travel lifts, hoists and davits whose steel sections need periodic crack checks, and the same goes for the rigging and shackles on working vessels.

Away from the water, MT is used on the carbon steel welds of fabricated frames and structural connections in the region's building work, on lugs and nozzle attachment welds of steel tanks and vessels at utility and process plants, and on the steel parts of airport ground support equipment. After a hurricane, owners often ask for a crack check on cranes, light-pole bases and steel supports that have taken wind load. The common thread is carbon steel with a stress concentration and a reason to worry about a surface crack.

What MT detects and what it does not

When a ferromagnetic part is magnetized, a crack at or near the surface distorts the field and leaks flux into the air. Fine magnetic particles dusted or sprayed on the surface collect at that leakage and outline the flaw. MT is quick, sensitive to tight cracks, and shows the flaw where it sits on the part. It finds surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams and lack of fusion, and flaws just beneath the surface.

The method is limited to ferromagnetic material. Carbon and low-alloy steels respond; austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, bronze and most marine fittings in those alloys do not, so a yacht tower or an aluminum hull needs penetrant testing instead. MT does not measure thickness and does not see deep internal flaws. Rust, heavy marine growth and thick coatings degrade sensitivity, and in Miami the typical surface needs real preparation before a particle will stick where it should.

Technique: yokes, prods, particles and light

Field MT usually starts with an alternating-current electromagnetic yoke. Before use it must show it can lift a test weight: ASME Section V Article 7 calls for at least 10 pounds at maximum pole spacing for AC yokes and at least 40 pounds for DC or permanent-magnet yokes. The area between the legs is magnetized and examined, then re-examined with the yoke turned about ninety degrees so cracks in either direction are caught. Prods push current through the part and cover larger areas, but they can leave arc burns, so procedures restrict them.

Particles come in dry powder and wet suspension. Dry powder in a contrasting color suits rough weld surfaces and warm conditions; wet particles give finer sensitivity and are preferred for fatigue-critical details. Fluorescent particles need UV-A light in a darkened enclosure, which in Miami's bright sun means a shroud or tent, and white-light levels for visible particles are measured, not guessed. A flux-direction check, such as a field indicator, proves the field is present before anything is accepted, and the part is demagnetized afterward if residual magnetism could affect later work.

Preparing marine and outdoor steel for MT

Surface preparation decides sensitivity. Corrosion products and mill scale hold the yoke legs away from the steel and weaken the field, and scale at a weld toe hides the very crack MT is looking for. Salt contamination makes steel absorb moisture and rust again within hours, so cleaning and examination should follow each other closely. Weld spatter, heavy ripple and undercut collect particles and must be dressed or acknowledged as limits. Grease and oily residue make particles streak and clump.

Where a coating stays on, the procedure sets the maximum thickness and requires a check that sensitivity survived, either with a known flaw or a field indicator. Marine paint systems are often thicker than that limit, so crews should expect to remove coating locally at the examination area. Rope, lanyards and temporary rigging near a lifting examination also need to be moved so the full weld length and its heat-affected zone are visible.

Lifting gear and fatigue cracks

Most of the cracks MT finds on lifting equipment start at a stress concentration: the toe of a fillet weld on a padeye, the radius at the root of a hook, the thread run-out of a pin, the corner of a cutout in a boom. Repeated loading opens them slowly, and a salt-laden atmosphere speeds the process by pitting the surface where the crack begins. The technician looks first at those places, magnetizes across the likely crack direction, and then repeats the examination at the right angle so nothing is missed.

Wire rope, chain and slings are not part of an MT scope, but the metal hardware at their ends is. A loaded component should be tested out of service where possible, because a crack that is closed under load can open once the load is released and show better. Findings on lifting gear are reported plainly to the owner or operator, who decides on removal from service under the applicable crane and rigging rules.

Residual magnetism and demagnetizing

A part that has been magnetized for testing can keep a residual field, and on a marine or process component that field has consequences. It pulls steel swarf onto bearing surfaces, deflects the arc during later welding, and disturbs compasses and magnetic instruments near a vessel. The procedure states when demagnetizing is required and how the result is checked with a field meter or an indicator, and the report records that the check was done.

On large fabrications, demagnetizing is often done by reducing the field of an AC yoke slowly while it is drawn away from the part, or by passing the part through a coil. Welded repairs on a magnetized part can show arc blow, so in Miami yard work the sequence of testing, demagnetizing and repair welding is agreed beforehand with the welding supervisor.

Codes and acceptance criteria for MT in Florida

MT is carried out to the code that governs the part. ASME Section V Article 7 defines the technique, supported by ASTM E709 and E1444. ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 6, holds the MT method and acceptance for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 covers magnetic particle examination of process piping with Table 341.3.2 for acceptance, and AWS D1.1 covers structural welds. Steel bridges for the state transportation department follow AWS D1.5.

The state also matters on pressure equipment: Florida's Boiler Safety Program, administered by the Division of State Fire Marshal under chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes, covers boilers, and facilities handling regulated chemicals face OSHA process safety management under 29 CFR 1910.119. For in-service tanks, vessels and piping under API 653, 510 and 570, the owner's authorized inspector decides what the findings mean, and we provide the examination records.

Who performs and approves the work

Atlantis keeps no staff or premises in Miami. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope and work under the company's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up, examines and interprets; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The reviewing Level III for Miami work is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer holds the certification responsibility, so the technician's record is traceable to the written practice cited in the report.

If you need a written practice or a code-specific MT procedure for your own staff, see our written practice development service.

What the MT report contains

The report lists the component and its position on the structure or vessel, the procedure and revision, the equipment (yoke or prods), the particle type, vehicle and concentration for wet work, the light measurement, and the yoke lift check or field-direction verification. It names the technician, level and date. Every indication is recorded with location, orientation and length and given an accept or reject decision against the cited table. Photographs and sketches mark areas covered, and limitations such as inaccessible welds or coating that stayed in place are stated. Any re-examination after grinding or repair is referenced to the original indication.

Planning an MT job in Miami

Weather and corrosion set the rhythm in Miami. Sun-heated steel can exceed the range where particles behave properly, so crews often start early or work in shade. Humid mornings leave dew on steel, which prevents particles from moving freely until the surface is dried. Afternoon thunderstorms stop outdoor examinations quickly, and the hurricane season from June through November can postpone work or create a surge of storm-related checks, so keep a schedule that tolerates delay.

Port and airport sites require facility credentials arranged in advance, and crane inspections need coordination with the operator's lifting schedule and lockout. Boatyard work is shaped by tides, haul-out dates and hot-work permits. Because technicians are mobilized from outside the city, listing everything that needs checking in one scope, and stating who provides access, power and cleaning, saves repeat travel and avoids partial inspections.

MT, PT or UT for your Miami job

Use MT for surface and near-surface cracks in steel. Use penetrant testing in Miami for aluminum, stainless and bronze, and for any material where MT does not apply. Use ultrasonic testing in Miami for wall thickness and internal weld flaws. A single repair often calls for two methods. Our magnetic particle testing guide and the national MT page give further detail.

Training your own MT technicians

Employers who prefer in-house capability can enroll people in MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 courses. The NDT training page for Miami explains the format, and the Article 7 explainer is a useful primer on what the examination requires.

faq.q: What is MT inspection used for in Miami?
faq.a: It is used on carbon and low-alloy steel where a surface crack would matter: port crane structures, lifting gear, boat hoists, vessel attachment welds and structural connections. It shows cracks that are invisible to the eye on a weathered, corroded surface.

faq.q: Can MT inspect aluminum boats or stainless yacht hardware?
faq.a: No. Aluminum and austenitic stainless steel are not ferromagnetic, so the particles cannot show a flaw. Penetrant testing is the surface method used on those materials, and it is common on marine welds and fittings.

faq.q: How does salt air affect magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Salt speeds rust and holds moisture on steel, so surfaces can degrade again soon after cleaning. Examination should follow preparation closely, and corroded or scaled areas must be cleaned back to sound metal for the field and particles to work.

faq.q: Do I need to remove marine paint before MT?
faq.a: Often in part. Thin, sound coatings can stay if the procedure permits and sensitivity is checked, but thick marine systems usually exceed the allowed limit and must be removed at the examination area. The report records the coating condition.

faq.q: Is fluorescent MT practical outdoors in Miami?
faq.a: It is possible with a darkened enclosure or shroud, because bright sun overwhelms UV-A light. Many field jobs use visible particles on rough surfaces and reserve fluorescent particles for fatigue-critical details that can be shaded or brought indoors.

faq.q: Can MT be done on cranes after a hurricane?
faq.a: Yes, as part of a post-storm check of welds, pins and structural connections on carbon steel. The owner or crane engineer defines the scope, and MT shows whether wind or impact loading has initiated surface cracks at stress concentrations.

faq.q: Which code controls MT acceptance on my Florida project?
faq.a: The code that governs the part decides: ASME Section VIII or B31.3 for pressure equipment and piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, AWS D1.5 for bridges, or the owner specification. The procedure and report cite the edition used.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Miami facility?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized to your site with their equipment and a Level III approved procedure. We spell out travel and access arrangements in the quote and agree who provides power, lifts and cleaning before the visit.

faq.q: Can I train technicians in MT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 training with practice questions and a simulator route. The employer certifies its technicians under its written practice, and the course supports that qualification process.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Miami, FL | Liquid PT
pt.description: On-site liquid penetrant testing of aluminum, stainless and steel welds for Miami marine, food and utility work. Visible and fluorescent PT. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Miami, Florida
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing (PT, or dye penetrant inspection) in Miami, Florida. PT finds cracks, porosity and laps that are open to the surface of welds, castings and machined parts, and it works on aluminum, stainless steel, bronze and other non-magnetic metals that Miami's marine and food industries rely on. Technicians are mobilized to your yard, plant or shop with materials and a written procedure for the agreed scope. Request a PT quote for Miami with the material, finish and governing code. We reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Miami

South Florida builds and repairs a large number of boats, and many of them are aluminum or stainless. Welded T-tops, towers, rails, fuel tanks and hull seams on yachts and workboats are routine PT subjects, as are stainless fittings and exhaust components. The marine yards along the Miami River and the refit operations around the port see a constant stream of cracked welds that need to be proven sound after grinding and repair. A penetrant check is the usual way to show that a repair cavity is clean before it is welded and again after it is finished.

On land, food and beverage plants and cold-storage facilities handling imported seafood, produce and dairy use stainless steel piping and tanks with sanitary welds. Hotels, hospitals and data centers run stainless and copper-alloy mechanical systems. Water and wastewater plants use bronze and stainless pump parts and valve bodies. Airport ground support equipment includes a lot of welded aluminum. In all of these, PT is the straightforward way to check for surface cracks in a material that magnetic methods cannot handle.

What PT shows and what it misses

Penetrant is a thin liquid that is drawn into surface-breaking flaws by capillary action. After the excess is removed, a developer pulls the liquid back out and spreads it into a visible indication. PT shows cracks, porosity and laps open to the surface, regardless of the metal, and it gives a result that can be photographed and kept. It is particularly good on smooth, clean welds and machined surfaces.

It does not find anything below the surface and it gives no information about wall thickness. Flaws that have been closed by grinding, blasting, brushing or peening may not accept penetrant. Rough, porous or heavily oxidized surfaces trap liquid and create false indications. Salt residue, oil and old paint block the flaw and need removal first. In Miami's environment, chlorides and humidity also complicate the cleaning and drying steps, so the procedure has to control them rather than assume them away.

Technique: from cleaning to evaluation

The sequence is simple, but each step has a purpose. The technician cleans the area and lets the solvent flash off. Penetrant is applied and left to dwell for the time the procedure sets for the material and flaw type. The excess is removed by solvent wipe, water wash or an emulsifier step depending on the system, taking care not to over-remove from shallow cracks. A thin, even coat of developer follows, and the technician inspects during and after the development time.

Visible dye is judged in white light at a measured minimum intensity; fluorescent penetrant is judged under UV-A light in a darkened area and gives better sensitivity to fine cracks. Indications are classed by type and size and compared with the code. The surface is cleaned again afterward, which matters on stainless steel piping where residue can affect later welding or service and on aluminum components where chloride-bearing materials are a concern.

Cleaning, chlorides and marine contamination

Miami surfaces carry salt. A weld that has sat outdoors for a week holds chloride, moisture and biological growth, and all of them can block penetrant entry or leave misleading residues. The cleaning step therefore goes beyond wiping: degreasing, removal of corrosion product, and in some cases a fresh-water rinse followed by complete drying. Where grinding or blasting has smeared metal over a crack, a light etch may be called for before penetrant goes on.

Stainless steel and nickel alloys bring a second concern. Specifications often limit halogens and sulfur in penetrant, remover and developer, because residues can attack the metal later. The procedure names the product family and the lot numbers go into the report. Technicians should not use general-purpose cleaners from site stores unless the procedure allows them, and wipes and rags should be disposed of as the facility requires.

Typical PT scopes for Miami owners

A few scopes recur. A refit yard may ask for PT on the root and cap of every weld in a new aluminum fuel tank or on the repair of a cracked tower or rail. A food plant may order PT on a run of new stainless process pipe before it is commissioned. A pump overhaul shop may check the sealing faces and fillets of bronze and stainless castings. After a repair, the owner may want proof that a ground-out crack cavity is clear before welding and that the finished weld is free of surface cracks, which means two examinations and two entries in the report.

Reading indications and judging them

Indications start to show as soon as the developer dries, and a technician watches them form. A thin, continuous line suggests a crack, a row of tiny dots a tight linear flaw or porosity, and a broad stain a rough surface or poor removal. Because marine surfaces are rarely smooth, the technician must tell a true indication from a weld ripple or a pit that holds liquid, and may re-clean and re-test an area to be sure.

Real indications are measured and compared with the code table for length, type and spacing. Cracks are rejected by most construction codes at any size, while rounded indications are accepted up to stated limits. The report cites the table used, so an owner can see how close an accepted indication was to the limit and plan the next inspection interval.

Codes and acceptance criteria for PT in Florida

ASME Section V Article 6 defines the examination, and ASTM E165 is the general-industry practice behind it. For pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 8 gives PT method and acceptance; for process piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 calls for liquid penetrant examination, with Table 341.3.2 setting acceptance. AWS D1.1 allows PT in some structural applications and AWS D1.6 covers stainless structures. Marine and owner specifications often add their own limits.

Boilers in Florida fall under the Boiler Safety Program of the Division of State Fire Marshal, which enforces the Boiler Safety Act in chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes and Rule 69A-51, and plants handling covered chemicals are subject to OSHA process safety management in 29 CFR 1910.119. In-service vessels and piping are examined under API 510 and 570 with the owner's authorized inspector in charge, and our PT reports are written so that inspector can use them directly.

Documenting repairs: before and after

Repair welding is where PT is used most often on Miami marine and mechanical work, and the record matters as much as the test. The first examination proves the excavated cavity is free of crack remnants, which stops a repair being welded over a flaw that was only partly removed. The second examination covers the finished weld and the surrounding heat-affected zone. Photographs taken at each stage, with a scale and a reference mark, let the owner, the surveyor or an insurer see the sequence without returning to the site.

Who performs and approves the work

We have no Miami office; technicians are mobilized to site for the agreed scope. They work under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. On Miami jobs that Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. The employer holds certification responsibility under SNT-TC-1A, which is why each report references the written practice and the technician's current level.

What the PT report contains

Each report states the component and its location, the procedure and revision, and the penetrant system by manufacturer, type and method, with the batch numbers of penetrant, remover and developer. It records the surface temperature, cleaning method, dwell time, developer time and light level, and names the technician and level. Indications are described by type, location and length with photographs, and marked accept or reject against the cited criteria. Areas that could not be examined are listed with reasons. Re-examination after repair uses the same procedure and is tied to the original report number.

Planning a PT job in Miami

The main constraint is temperature. The standard working window in Article 6 of ASME Section V is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for both the surface and the penetrant materials, and the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature if work falls outside it. Sun-exposed aluminum and steel in Miami routinely exceed 125 degrees by midday, so crews often examine early, shade the work, or cool the surface before penetrant goes on. Penetrant that dries on a hot surface cannot be removed properly and produces false indications.

Humidity, afternoon storms and sea spray affect cleaning and drying. Fluorescent examination in daylight needs a shroud. Vessel work needs hot-work and confined-space arrangements, gas-free certificates for tanks, and coordination with the yard schedule and tides. Because technicians travel to Miami, confirm that the facility accepts the solvents and waste handling in the procedure, and settle who provides access, power and lifts beforehand.

PT, MT or UT for your Miami job

Choose PT for aluminum, stainless steel, bronze and other non-magnetic materials and for fine cracks on machined or ground surfaces. Choose magnetic particle testing in Miami when the part is steel and speed matters, and ultrasonic testing in Miami for remaining wall or flaws inside a weld. Our comparison of MT and PT and the national penetrant testing page explain the trade-offs in more detail.

Training your own PT technicians

Miami employers who want in-house PT capability can send staff through PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 courses and practice on the Practical NDT penetrant simulator. The NDT training page for Miami describes the format, and the Article 6 explainer is good preparation.

faq.q: Can PT be used on aluminum boat welds in Miami?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant testing works on aluminum and is the usual surface method for welded aluminum boat structures. The area must be clean and dry, and the temperature must be inside the procedure limits for the penetrant materials to behave properly.

faq.q: What does dye penetrant testing find?
faq.a: It finds cracks, porosity, laps and seams that are open to the surface. It will not detect flaws below the surface, and it does not measure thickness, so a weld that needs volume examination is also checked by UT.

faq.q: Does salt contamination affect penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Salt, moisture and growth on marine surfaces can block penetrant from entering a crack or leave misleading residues. The procedure requires thorough cleaning, sometimes a fresh-water rinse, and complete drying before penetrant is applied.

faq.q: Are penetrant materials restricted on stainless steel?
faq.a: Often. Specifications commonly limit halogens and sulfur in the penetrant, remover and developer used on stainless steel and nickel alloys. The procedure names compliant products and the report lists the lot numbers used.

faq.q: Is it too hot for PT in Miami?
faq.a: It can be. The standard window is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit under Article 6 of ASME Section V, and sunlit metal often exceeds that. Crews shade or cool the surface, work early, or use a procedure qualified for the higher temperature.

faq.q: Visible or fluorescent penetrant for marine welds?
faq.a: Visible dye suits general field work in good light. Fluorescent penetrant gives higher sensitivity for fine cracks but needs UV-A light in a darkened area, so it is chosen when the code or the criticality of the part calls for it.

faq.q: What happens after a PT indication is found?
faq.a: The indication is measured, evaluated against the code criteria, and reported as accept or reject. If it is rejected, the owner decides on repair; after grinding and welding the same procedure is used for re-examination and the results are linked to the first report.

faq.q: Does Atlantis run a Miami shop or crew?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized to the site for the agreed scope with equipment and a Level III approved procedure. The quote sets out travel, access and permit needs, and we confirm responsibilities before the visit.

faq.q: Can my staff be trained in penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and Level 2 courses supported by practice questions and a simulator. Certification is the employer's responsibility under its written practice, and the course supplies the training element of that record.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in Miami, FL
rt.description: Radiography is not an Atlantis service in the US. Miami options: UT as a volumetric alternative, Level III radiograph review and RT training. Get a quote.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Options in Miami, Florida
rt.html:
Anyone searching for radiographic testing in Miami should know the position up front. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing for any customer in the United States. Industrial radiography is licensed work, regulated under the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not part of our service. The rest of this page sets out the help available to a Miami owner whose specification asks for radiographic examination.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative

Ultrasonic examination looks through the weld volume without radiation, so there are no exclusion zones to clear on a busy dock, in an occupied building or beside a vessel under repair. Ultrasonic testing in Miami covers shear-wave weld examination and thickness work. Substitution has conditions. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 sets its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only in specific circumstances.

Because of that, the change is settled with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job. We can prepare the technical justification, setting out joint geometry, material, thickness and the code clause relied on, so that the decision is recorded and not left to the field.

Level III review of radiographs, no radiation licence needed

Checking a radiograph does not involve a source, so it needs no radiation licence. An ASNT Level III from Atlantis reviews film or digital images and the technique sheet against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, gives a second opinion on disputed indications, and checks image quality indicators, density and coverage. The same Level III can review an RT contractor's procedure and written practice. The reviewer is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Most of this is desk work from the records, so travel is seldom required.

Owners use this when a contractor hands over radiographs and they want an independent view before accepting a weld, and contractors use it to have a procedure checked before bidding. The Level III consulting page explains how an engagement is arranged.

Surface methods that sit alongside UT

Radiography and UT both examine the volume. Surface-breaking flaws and weld toe cracks are better found by magnetic particle testing in Miami on steel and by penetrant testing in Miami on aluminum, stainless steel and bronze. A package that pairs UT for the weld volume with MT or PT for the surface can cover the ground that radiography and visual examination would together.

RT training and written practice

Technicians who need the theory of radiography can study it in our RT Level 2 course, which covers physics, film and image quality, and interpretation to code. Practical exposure work and radiation safety qualification are arranged by the employer under its own licence, and the employer certifies its personnel under its written practice. See the NDT training page for Miami for the course structure, and written practice development for help building the program.

How to request what you need

Tell us the weld type, material, thickness, code and edition, and whether the contract demands radiography itself or only a volumetric method. We will tell you whether UT is credible, whether a radiograph review is what you need, or whether you must go to a licensed radiography contractor. Request a quote for Miami and we reply within one business day. For any field work, technicians are mobilized to your site, as we keep no office in Miami.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Miami?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not carry out radiography at any US site, Miami included, because it is licensed work under 10 CFR Part 34 or an Agreement State program. The services on offer are UT, Level III radiograph review and RT training.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on a Florida weld?
faq.a: Sometimes, if the construction code and the owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and, under conditions, ASME Section VIII address ultrasonic examination. Agree the substitution with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector first.

faq.q: Can someone independent review radiographs from my contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the code, give a second read on disputed indications, and review the contractor's procedure and written practice.

faq.q: Can my team study radiographic testing theory with Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes, through the RT Level 2 course covering theory and interpretation. Practical exposure and radiation safety qualification are arranged by the employer under its licence, and the employer certifies personnel under its written practice.

faq.q: Will Atlantis refer me to a radiography contractor in Miami?
faq.a: No, we do not name or recommend radiography contractors. If your contract requires radiography, select a contractor holding the right licence for the state, and check their credentials and procedure before work begins.
